items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: when I got to meet Dizzy it was with Marshall. And I remember Marshall talking to Dizzy.

ctx.x: Did you personally have — I don’t want to say a problem — how did you adjust in your thinking and listening to the bop movement?

Oh that was a kind of an interesting thing because I was already aware of what was beginning to happen before the war. You see I got drafted straight off the campus, I was inducted about two or three months after I graduated from Yale. The first inkling was in the form of Dizzy Gillespie’s playing. And I first heard Dizzy in I guess it was 1938 because I remember discussing it with Marshall Stearns. His records came out and there were solos of Dizzy’s on various releases, including of course the Cab Calloway…

discharged relatively early, in fact he got discharged when his squadron was brought back to the United States from Europe in order to fly out immediately to Japan and then they were told when they were ready to go, well we don’t need you out there and those of you who have had enough service can get discharged. And that’s when he married my sister and moved out to Los Angeles, his home. items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Oh, he was like that, from the first time that I met him with the Calloway band before the war.

ctx.x: He really was as happy as he . . .

Oh, he was like that, from the first time that I met him with the Calloway band before the war. I must have met Milt Hinton, but I don’t remember him. Milt doesn’t remember. He says, “Oh yeah, we played New Haven lots of times.” That’s where I first met Benny Carter, for example, when he came back out of his long stay in Europe, where he became music director of the BBC.

What you said before is interesting, because it reminded me of something that Eddie Heywood said. When you came back after the war and heard this new music, that’s when Eddie said he felt that the war was really responsible for the sudden void, the step backwards for jazz, because there was no transitional period for the public, that it . . .
